Bachelor's Thesis Seminar Econometrics - Research Project

description.contents: Topics covered in the course are:elementary macroeconomic facts and concepts (such as national accounting, deflators and Okun’s Law);static general equilibrium models for closed and small open economies;neoclassical business cycle theory (the IS-LM model, the Mundell-Fleming model, the AD-AS model, the Phillips-curve and the Lucas-critique);illustrations and applications from the recent macroeconomic history.
description.objectives: After successful completion of this course, students will be able:to explain the most important macroeconomic variables;to analyse in how the economy reacts to changes in government purchases, taxes or the money supply;to interpret events in the macroeconomic history since World War II;to explain static general equilibrium models for closed and small open economies;to explain the (quantitative) relation between the monetary system, inflation and unemployment according to the classic macroeconomic theory;to explain neoclassical business cycle theory and to discuss its basic Keynesian building blocks;to analyse and quantify the impact of shocks in the different macroeconomic models.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Econometrics and Data Science and B Actuarial Science.

description.contents: This course is an introduction to calculus at the academic level. Basic topics from classical differential calculus and integration theory are discussed using Stewart’s book Calculus: Early Transcendentals. During the lectures, a general introduction to the theory is given. The tutorials will elaborate on the theoretical insights through discussion of exercises and further applications. Topics: sequences and series, geometric series;functions: absolute value, polynomials, rational functions, exponential functions, logarithms, (arc)sine, (arc)cosine and (arc)tangent;properties of functions: (co)domain, range, increasing and decreasing, concave and convex, injective and surjective;limits of functions, continuity and intermediate value theorem;derivative as a limit, rules of differentiation, implicit and logarithmic differentiation, linear approximation and differentials;curve sketching to investigate functions, critical points, local and global extrema, mean value theorem, asymptotes and l’Hôpital’s rule;Riemann-integrals, interpretation of integrals in terms of areas and anti-derivatives;(in)determinate integral forms and improper integrals;fundamental theorem of calculus and applications in terms of calculating integrals;integration techniques: integration by substitution, integration by parts and integration of rational functions by partial fractions.
description.objectives: This course aims to deepen a basic understanding of functions as mathematical objects and their properties. Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: demonstrate the validity of mathematical statements using important theorems and definitions from single-variable calculus;analyze mathematical functions using their main characteristics;apply various differentiation techniques;analyze limiting behaviour of sequences and functions and calculate limits on the basis of theoretical notions of convergence and limit rules;apply various important theorems from single-variable calculus;analyze the convergence of (in)definite and improper Riemann-integrals of (almost) continuous functions and relate this to differential calculus;apply various integration techniques to calculate (in)definite integrals.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Econometrics and Data Science, B Actuarial Science and B Business Analytics.

description.contents: The first two weeks are spent on mathematical methods needed to perform a thorough analysis of microeconomic models. In this respect, the following topics are covered: differentiation of functions of several variables, partial derivatives and continuity, gradient, directional derivatives, optimisation, and Lagrange’s Theorem.In the next four weeks, economic phenomena are explained by microeconomic models. For each model, three essential components are distinguished: the economic actors and their motivation, the economic environment, and the assumptions underlying the models. The course will focus on the theory of consumer behaviour and the derivation of the demand curve, the theory of producer behaviour and the derivation of the supply curve, market forces under different assumptions, game theory, and externalities. We also will be discussing how political bodies like governments may influence markets in order to achieve different market outcomes; Pareto-efficiency will be the leading principle here.
description.objectives: After successful completion of the course, students will be able to:the student can calculate partial derivatives and gradients of standard multivariate functions;the student can optimise functions of 2 variables, and provide necessary and sufficient conditions for a local extremum;the student can put up microeconomic models for the consumer and solve the consumer utility optimisation problem graphically, and by using Lagrange's technique;the students can put up microeconomic models for the producer and solve its optimisation problems, graphically and using Lagrange's technique;the student is able to calculate equilibria in competitive markets by deriving supply and demand curves;student can evaluate market outcomes in terms of Pareto optimality;the students can provide different instruments for a political body to influence market outcomes;the student can analyse monopoly and compare it with perfect competition;the student can give examples of positive and negative externalities in various microeconomic contexts and provide possible measures as solutions to the externality problem;the student can apply the Nash equilibrium concept from game theory to study equilibria in oligopolistic competition.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Econometrics and Data Science, B Actuarial Science or B Business Analytics.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: Calculus at the level of Mathematics 1: Calculus.

description.contents: The student acquires a solid understanding of probability theory, which will serve as an indispensable basis for many subsequent courses in the programme. During the lectures, all of the below-mentioned topics will be discussed step-by-step, starting with the axioms of probability theory. Proofs of theorems will be provided, and examples will be discussed. The students prepare for each tutorial by solving a number of exercises. During these tutorials, the exercises will be discussed by the teacher and will serve as an illustration of applications of the theory. In these classes, there will be ample time for raising questions and discussion. Sometimes, a part of the tutorial will be used to discuss an important theory.Topics: descriptive statistics (measuring scales, mode, median, average, variance, percentile, graphical techniques);population and random sampling;experiments, outcome space and events;definitions of probability and axioms of probability theory;conditional probability, independence and Bayes’ Theorem;combinatorics, counting techniques, permutations, combinations and binomial theorem;sampling with or without replacement;discrete versus continuous random variables, PDF and CDF;expectation, variance and (higher) moments;inequalities of Markov, Chebychev and Jensen;probability generating functions and moment generating functions;specific discrete distributions and their properties: uniform, binomial, hypergeometric, geometric, negative-binomial and Poisson distribution; Poisson processes;specific continuous distributions: uniform, exponential, gamma, chi-squared and normal distribution, as well as approximations with the normal distribution of discrete distributions and other distributions;univariate transformations, PDF-, CDF- and MGF-methods;inverse CDF method for the generation of random variables from a desired distribution;location and scale parameters.
description.objectives: After successful completion of the course, students will be able to:apply the most important techniques in descriptive statistics;derive the proofs of important theorems in probability theory and combinatorics;apply theorems of important results in probability theory;analyse and solve probability problems;derive and apply the main univariate probability distributions;derive probabilities, expected values, variances, moment generating functions for any given probability or density function;derive probability distributions using transformations of univariate random variables.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Econometrics and Data Science, B Actuarial Science, B Business Analytics, or BSc Politics, Psychology, Law and Economics.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: Calculus at the level of Mathematics 1: Calculus .

description.contents: The main objective of this course is to provide the student with a solid basis of computer programming as an indispensable skill for the remaining study in econometrics and actuarial science.Much attention will be paid to the development of so-called algorithmic thinking, by which the student will be endowed with the skill of structuring and solving mathematical problems in a systematic way. Designing algorithms for (simple) mathematical problems is irrespective of a specific programming language. One’s own algorithms will be implemented in a program so that the algorithm can be executed and verified. Apart from translating an algorithm into a computer language, attention will be paid to a number of numerical methods.Specific topics are:floating-point number representations;root finding;interpolation using: Lagrange polynomials;numerical integration: Riemann sums, Simpson's rule, Monte Carlo;automatic differentiation.
description.objectives: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:use the fundamental syntax, object types and control flow in Python;translate a mathematical problem into an algorithm;apply and implement numerical algorithms;test and debug Python functions;apply basic object-oriented programming concepts;articulate and justify the reasoning behind their solutions to programming problems.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Econometrics and Data Science and B Actuarial Science.
description.requiredPriorKnowledge: Elementary analysis as covered in Mathematics 1: Calculus.

description.contents: This course offers a broad introduction to modern finance, theoretical and empirical. Central topics are the assessment of investment projects and the way to finance them (equity or debt). The course also covers the fundamental relationship between risk and return by presenting modern portfolio theory and the capital asset pricing model (CAPM): the most important and widely applied model in finance. During this course the following topics will be addressed:introduction to financial accounting;capital budgeting;valuation of bonds and stocks;risk and returns;CAPM-model;theories of capital structure;the effect of taxation;the influence of market imperfections.
description.objectives: After successful completion of this course, students will be able to: perform a financial statement analysis and estimate cash flows;assess the risk and time value of investments, including stocks, bonds and entire corporations;make capital budget decisions on whether to invest in a project based on different investment decision rules;apply the capital asset pricing model (CAPM);make capital structure decisions;analyse the effect of taxation on capital structure and investment decisions;explain the basic types of firms and the role of ownership.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Econometrics and Data Science, B Actuarial Science, B Business Analytics or Schakelprogramma Data Science and Business Analytics

description.contents: The main objective of this course is to provide the student with a solid basis of linear algebra as indispensable knowledge for the remaining study in econometrics and actuarial science.Topics addressed in the course are:vector geometry: line, surface, normal, direction vector, angle, unit vector, inner product, outer product, norm, length, distance, triangular inequality and inequality of Cauchy-Schwarz;matrices: systems of linear equations, matrix algebra, Gauss-Jordan elimination, and inverse;linear transformations: transformation matrix, projection, reflection and rotation;subspaces: kernel and image, independence, basis, dimension and rank theorem;coordinates, coordinate transformations, diagonalisation and similarity;determinants: patterns, properties, Laplace expansion, geometric interpretation of the determinant of transformations in R2, R3 and Cramer’s rule;transition matrices.
description.objectives: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:use vector geometry in order to analyse and solve geometric problems;apply matrix algebra for solving systems of linear equations and determine the kernel and image of a matrix as related to solutions of homogeneous and non-homogeneous systems;apply the concepts of linear subspaces, linear independence, bases and dimension;apply matrix algebra to describe linear transformations in terms of the corresponding transformations matrix and with respect to different bases;analyse determinants.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Econometrics and Data Science, B Actuarial Science, B Business Analytics and PPLE.

description.contents: Orientation Econometrics:When gasoline prices are increasing, more people will use trains to commute to their work. And when mortgage rates are decreasing, house prices will increase. These are apparently obvious relations between economic variables but are these consistent with reality, and if so, can we quantify these effects? These kinds of questions belong to the core of the profession of an econometrician. A research study is conducted by collecting useful data, which they then analyse using statistical models and methods to quantify the economic relations under investigation. The work of an econometrician consists of the empirical testing of economic theory, making forecasts and evaluating potential policy objectives. This course summarises the techniques necessary to do so and will start with the application of it to a number of simple research problems.Orientation Actuarial Science:A life actuary analyses questions such as: how much should we pay for our pension benefits, and what should our retirement age be in the future? On the non-life side, actuaries analyse big datasets from insurance companies e.g., to construct risk-based premiums. Using risk factors in generalised linear regression models results in risk classification: which policyholders are good, and which are bad risks? It is critical for the actuary to be able to provide management with this type of information, based on advanced probabilistic and statistical techniques. Besides predicting the expected losses, actuaries are also interested in quantifying the uncertainty in the losses. Further, insurance companies and pension funds have huge assets under management. Simply investing these in the financial market can result in volatile asset returns. Derivatives can be used to hedge against these volatile movements, and the pricing of such derivatives will be illustrated.Skills:The Skills segment will be about conducting empirical research and writing a scientific research report. The topics which will be discussed are the characteristics of academic texts, the use of a standard text scheme, the use of economic theory and relevant literature, the design of a research project, the presentation, and analysis of the results and the evaluation of the research project.
description.objectives: This course consists of two Orientation segments and a Skills segment.Orientation segment Econometrics:The student will also learn how to implement calculations and estimations during computer classes.Orientation segment Actuarial Science:This segment is designed to offer students a notion about general topics in the fields of Actuarial Science, Mathematical Finance and Quantitative Risk Management.The student will also learn how to implement calculations in the aforementioned fields using MS Excel and R during the computer lab sessions.Skills segment:The Skills segment will be about conducting empirical research and writing a scientific research report.Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:the student can explain basic concepts of econometrics, such as linear regression, testing of parameters, unbiasedness, consistency, and efficiency;the student is able to carry out both explorative analyses of economic data using simple statistical models and analyses of economic relations independently;the student can explain basic topics in Life Insurance, such as calculations of premiums and technical provisions for simple life insurance contracts;the student can explain basic topics in Financial Mathematics, such as the equivalence principle for cash-flows, and option pricing by replication and change of measure;the student is able to design and conduct an empirical research project;the student is able to analyse and judge the results of empirical research;the student can write a report about the conducted research;the student is able to explain the role and responsibility of econometricians and actuarians in and towards a fair and sustainable society;the student is able to use R to conduct a regression analysis;the student is able to write a literature review;the student is able to work effectively in a group.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Econometrics and Data Science or B Actuarial Science.

description.contents: After creating a sound theoretical basis, the theory will be extended step-by-step in the course, proofs of the theorems will be given, and examples will be discussed extensively. The exercises included in the reader are an essential part of the course to get acquainted with the presented theory. The students prepare for each tutorial by solving a number of exercises. During these tutorials, the teacher will discuss the exercises and serve as an illustration of the applications of the theory. There will also be time for raising questions and discussion.Topics:multiple integrals, Fubini's Theorem, coordinate transformations;multivariate distributions, joint pdf and CDF and marginal distributions;independence of random variables, covariance and correlation;conditional distributions, expectations and variances;variance-covariance matrix;simultaneous moment generation functions;multinomial and bivariate normal distribution;multivariate transformations: CDF, transformation, and mgf method;distributions of sums of random variables and convolution formula;T and F distribution;random samples: empirical CDF, sample statistics, distribution of sample statistics for samples from normal and binomial distributions;application to order statistics;point estimators, confidence intervals and hypothesis testing for population mean, population variance and population proportion, as well as for differences of those parameters between two populations;power and p-value.
description.objectives: Upon successful completion of this course, the students will be able to:student is able to apply basic integration techniques in multivariable calculus;student is able to apply the important theorems and definitions of multivariate probability theory;student is able to apply theorems to develop (simple) proofs for results in probability theory and statistics;the student is able to derive probabilities, (conditional) expected values and variances and simultaneous moment-generating functions for any given simultaneous distribution (discrete or continuous);the student is able to derive probability distributions of transformations of multivariate random variables and thus also of the most common sampling distributions, including order statistics;the student is able to apply techniques of estimation theory (including confidence intervals) for sampling from normal and binomial distributions, as well as estimation of differences between two populations;the student is able to apply the fundamental principles of hypothesis testing;the student is able to write code for a software package for (simple) simulation of random samples;the student is able to write a mathematical report in LaTeX.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Econometrics and Data Science, B Actuarial Science, B Business Analytics and BSc Politics, Psychology, Law and Economics.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: Probability Theory and Statistics 1 is highly recommended, as well as calculus at the level of Mathematics 1: Calculus.

description.contents: This course is composed of two parts: Data preprocessing and skills.Data preprocessing (part 1)The availability of large data sets, on the one hand, and increasing computer power, on the other hand, provides a new and valuable cocktail for companies. One of the big challenges is to use statistical software to extract information from the available data. This data, however, is often unrefined and incomplete. The first step in this statistical learning process is data wrangling (cleaning, transforming, merging and reshaping the data), which is one of the subjects of this course. Once the data is parsed and cleaned, exploratory data analysis provides information on the possible information content of the data and serves as a guide to select appropriate, more advanced, statistical and machine learning techniques. We also discuss and apply principal component analysis as a tool to reduce the dimensions of a data set containing many variables. After performing these analyses, advanced statistical methods can be used to further investigate the data. Although the details of these statistical learning techniques are part of other courses, we will provide the general mathematical framework behind statistical learning and data science, give an overview of the most important concepts (bias-variance tradeoff, regression function, training/testing error, overfitting, etc) used in data science and illustrate these concepts using the K-nearest neighbour algorithm.Skills (part 2)The central focus is on giving a presentation. The student will work on strengthening his/her academic presentation skills by the application of the theory to presentations in concrete situations. An academic presentation for larger audiences will usually form an integral part of the future profession.
description.objectives: This course is composed of two parts: Data preprocessing and skills. After finishing this course, the students will be able to:develop solutions to clean a data set that contains missing and wrong values;detect the normality of a variable;perform exploratory data analysis using software;calculate the principal components of a data set;recommend how to reduce the dimension of the data set;analyse the relation between the regression function and the goodness-of-fit measure;illustrate basic concepts of statistical learning using the K-nearest neighbour method;prepare and execute a presentation on a scientific topic;answer and ask critical questions;give and receive feedback;discuss possible ethical issues with data analysis.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Econometrics and Data Science, B Actuarial Science, or B Business Analytics.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: Probability theory and statistics at the level of Probability Theory and Statistics 1 and Probability Theory and Statistics 2 , Introduction Econometrics and Actuarial Science. Mathematics at the level of Mathematics 1: Calculus and Mathematics 2: Linear Algebra.

description.contents: The course covers the following topics:an introduction to life contingent risks and related financial products;a discrete-time framework to value cash flows over time with a discussion of discount functions, interest and discount rates, the actuarial equivalence of cash flow vectors, balances and reserves for a given cash flow vector and prospective and retrospective views;the life table, human mortality data and their characteristics, demographic markers, calculating probabilities using the data published in a life table and a discussion of different types of life tables;life annuity products, calculating actuarial present values and premiums;life insurance products, calculating actuarial present values and premiums;policy values for annuity and life insurance products, a general framework, recursions, and detailed insights;working with fractional durations;working in continuous time and extending all topics studied before from discrete to continuous settings;select mortality;expenses and profits.
description.objectives: After following this course, students will be able to:explain the main human mortality models and calculate the basic statistics of human mortality data;value life contingent liabilities where cash flows depend on the future lifetime of an insured;calculate actuarial present values, premium structures and policy values of life annuity and life insurance products;use the relevant international actuarial notation for life-contingent risks;model life insurance products in both discrete and continuous time;be aware of the societal impact of the technical concepts discussed in the course, e.g., in discussions related to the sustainability of pension systems or regarding the affordability of essential life insurance products.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Econometrics and Data Science, B Actuarial Science or the Minor Actuarial Science (30 EC) or Pre-master Actuarial Science and Mathematical Finance.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: The course recommends a basic understanding (at the level of the first year of a BSc in a quantitative study program) of algebra, analysis and probability theory.

description.contents: Concepts:orthogonality: projections, orthonormal bases and orthogonal transformations;polynomials and complex numbers: complex plane, complex conjugate, modulus of a complex number and complex polar coordinates;diagonalisation: eigenvalues and eigenvectors, linear dynamical systems;spectral theorem for symmetric and orthogonal matrices;quadratic forms and positive/negative (semi)definite matrices; singular value decomposition.Methods and results:Gram-Schmidt process, QR factorisation and least squares;diagonalisation theorem;fundamental theorem of algebra, conjugateness of complex roots of real polynomials.
description.objectives: After successful completion of this course, students will be able to:apply the concept of orthogonality;find best-fit solutions using least-squares approximations;diagonalize matrices to analyze the geometry of matrices;analyse basic properties of symmetric matrices and quadratic forms in terms of related theorems;analyse the singular value decomposition;apply complex numbers to study the roots of polynomials;use the software package Python to solve applied problems using linear algebra;demonstrate the validity of mathematical statements through formal arguments.

description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: Students are assumed to be familiar with the following concepts and techniques from Mathematics 2: Linear Algebra:matrix algebra: multiplication, inversion and calculating determinants;linear subspace, linear span, linear independence, basis and dimension;kernel and image of a linear transformation.

description.contents: Concepts:infinite sequences and series, especially power series and their applications;Taylor's Theorem (univariate and multivariate);Taylor series of well-known functions;derivatives, linear and quadratic approximations and the Hessian matrix;invertibility and local invertibility of a mapping;neighbourhood of a point, interior and boundary of a set;Lagrangian functions;convexity.Methods and results:Taylor's Theorem;convergence of sequences and series;theorem on necessary and sufficient conditions for local extrema;inverse and implicit function theorem;necessary and sufficient conditions for local extrema of unconstrained optimisation problems;necessary and sufficient conditions for local extrema of optimisation problems under equality and inequality constraints;convex programming and sufficient conditions for global extrema.
description.objectives: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:provide approximations of regular functions by Taylor polynomials, and estimate the error term;apply topological concepts and limits in higher dimensional Euclidean spaces to multivariate analysis;calculate derivatives of multivariate functions;prove the existence of local solutions to nonlinear systems of equations;explain how to solve (un)constrained and optimization problems and calculate solutions in small problems;solve convex optimization problems;demonstrate the validity of mathematical statements by formal arguments;find numerical solutions to (un)restricted optimization problems using;calculate the Taylor-series for well-known functions.

description.contents: limiting distributions, convergence in distribution and degenerate limiting distributions;Central Limit Theorem;asymptotic normality, convergence in probability and stochastic convergence;properties of estimators and unbiasedness;Cramer-Rao lower bound;uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimators;sufficiency;factorisation criterion;Rao-Blackwell 'improvement' theorem;Lehmann-Scheffe theorem;completeness;regular exponential class;confidence intervals and pivotal quantities;relation between tests and confidence intervals;significance level;simple/joint hypotheses;Neyman-Pearson lemma;uniformly most powerful tests;generalised likelihood ratio tests.
description.objectives: The student obtains fundamental insights into classical mathematical statistics and is able to work with basic statistical models. Upon completion of this course, students will be able to:the student is able to analyse various statistical convergence notions, including convergence in distribution and convergence in probability;the student is able to analyse the notions of stochastic convergence to investigate asymptotic normality;the student is able to derive estimators by means of the method of moments and the principle of maximum likelihood;the student is able to evaluate and compare point estimators based on the properties of these estimators (consistency, efficiency, relative efficiency);the student is able to analyse various methods for finding a 'uniform minimum variance unbiased estimator' (UMVUE) of a given parameter;the student is able to derive optimal estimators, confidence intervals and statistical hypothesis tests using the concepts of 'completeness' and 'sufficiency;the student is able to apply various statistical techniques to derive confidence intervals and statistical tests;the student is able to derive elementary properties of tests, such as the size and power of tests;the student is able to analyse several statistical methods to find uniform, most powerful tests;the student is able to derive and apply generalised likelihood ratio tests.

description.contents: This is an introductory-level course in supervised learning, focusing on regression and classification methods.Topics:bias-variance tradeoff and cross-validation;model selection in high dimensional regression;shrinkage (ridge and lasso) and dimension reduction methods;classification, discriminant analysis, logistic regression, and confusion matrix;nonlinear models and splines;tree-based methods, bagging, and random forests.
description.objectives: On completion of the course:the student is able to recognise the fundamental issues and challenges of statistical learning: data, model selection, model complexity;the student is able to explain the strengths and weaknesses of many popular statistical learning approaches;the student is able to implement various statistical learning algorithms in a range of real-world applications;the student is able to recommend appropriate statistical learning methods for a variety of problem scenarios;the student is able to discuss ethical considerations in algorithmic and statistical practices;the student is able to attain proficiency in Python programming for statistical learning applications.

description.contents: The course gives a rigorous introduction to applied and theoretical econometrics. The course discusses how applied econometrics can be used to estimate important quantities, analyse economic outcomes such as policy changes, markets and individual behaviour, and test theories and predict using econometric models. We discuss how various empirical problems directed the development of new econometric techniques. It is shown how different model specifications and variable transformations are used to obtain models that can be used to investigate various economic phenomena.The theory part of the course provides the foundation of the econometric methodology around the linear multivariate regression model. We introduce the vector, matrix notation, and the corresponding matrix algebra as a unifying approach to building econometric models and estimators. Among other things, we discuss how these mathematical tools can be used to study the properties of the Ordinary Least Squares (LS) estimator under the classical model assumptions. Both exact (finite sample) and asymptotic approximations are used when establishing the properties of the OLS estimator. Statistical software packages STATA and R are used to illustrate the empirical and theoretical aspects of all discussed concepts in the course.
description.objectives: At the end of this course, the student: is able to specify the linear regression model with standard assumptions;is able to provide a statistical and economic interpretation of the results of an econometric analysis;is able to analyse the model specification in the case of nonlinear relation and interaction effects using the appropriate tests;is able to give the economic interpretation of different model formulations;is able to formulate hypotheses relevant to real-life data, carry out relevant estimation and tests to verify these hypotheses;is able to use matrix notation for model formulation and LS estimation;is able to analyse the quality of the LS estimators and the related t-, F-, W- test statistics;is able to adapt estimation and inference procedure in case of invalid classical model assumptions (e.g. heteroscedasticity;is able to carry out LS estimation and testing using R and STATA.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Econometrics and Data Science, B Actuarial Science, B Business Analytics, Minor Actuarial Science (30 EC), Minor Econometrics and Mathematical Economics, Pre-master Econometrics, Pre-master Actuarial Science and Mathematical Finance, Schakelprogramma Data Science and Business Analytics or B Mathematics.

This also holds for Business Analytics students (although the course does not belong to the mandatory program). For minor students requirements set by the program director must be met.

description.contents: Mathematical Economics is a mathematical, model-based approach to study the economy. Topics discussed are:theory of consumer behaviour (preferences, utility function, demand function, choice under uncertainty);theory of producer behaviour (production function, cost function and profit function);markets with perfect competition and partial equilibrium (monopoly, consumer surplus and welfare loss);general equilibrium (Pareto efficiency, Edgeworth box, Walrasian equilibrium and welfare theorems);game theory (strategy, games in strategic and extensive form, Nash equilibrium in pure and mixed strategies and subgame-perfect equilibrium).
description.objectives: After successful completion of this course, students will be:the student is able to explain the concept of preferences over certain and uncertain outcomes and relate those to utility theory;the student is able to solve a consumer's utility maximisation problem for standard classes of utility functions and discuss the properties of the solutions;the student is able to solve a consumer's expenditure maximisation problem and discuss the properties of the solutions;the student is able to explain the effect of price changes as the result of compensation schemes on consumer behavior and welfare;the student is able to solve a producer's long- and short-run cost minimisation and profit maximisation problem for standard classes of production technologies and discuss the properties of the solutions;the student is able to explain equilibrium concepts like Pareto efficient allocation and barter equilibrium in pure exchange economies visually and by calculations;the student is able to calculate and visualise Walrasian equilibria in small exchange economies;the student is able to explain the first and second welfare theorem;the student is able to calculate equilibria in small markets with perfect competition and monopoly;the student is able to find Nash equilibria and subgame perfect Nash equilibria in simple strategic and extensive form games;the student is able to formulate a simple strategic situation as a strategic form or extensive form game;the student is able to discuss ways to implement responsible and sustainable firm behavior by policies to deal with (negative) externalities;the student is able to explain the ethical meaning of the second welfare theorem in terms of inequality and ways to reduce it.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Econometrics and Data Science, B Actuarial Science, B Business Analytics, Pre-master Econometrics, Minor Econometrics and Mathematical Economics or BSc Mathematics.
description.requiredPriorKnowledge: Knowledge about multi-variate analysis is recommended at the level of Mathematics 4: Multivariate Analysis.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: Students are expected to be familiar with the following techniques to analyse and solve contrained optimisation problems: Lagrange optimisation, concave programming, envelope theorem, existence of global minima or maxima. Knowledge is assumed at the level of Mathematics 3: Advanced Linear Algebra and Mathematics 4: Multivariate Analysis.

description.contents: The course explains a number of fundamental concepts that are important for interpreting quantitative results: understanding endogeneity is crucial, but different models are appropriate for different data types. The course deals with measurement errors, simultaneous equation bias, self-selection, censoring, truncation, etc. These ideas can be clearly explained with econometric models. Using these models, tests can be derived, and solutions can be found for estimation and inference for the problems considered.Modelling itself is also an important skill, and the course provides initial techniques and extensions for the correct modelling of economic variables. We will consider:models with endogenous regressors (simultaneous equations, IV, GMM);non-linear methods, including NLS and Maximum Likelihood;models for discrete choices and other limited dependent variables (including (multinomial) Logit/Probit, Tobit, and selection- models);estimation and testing of the above models in practice (using the computer and appropriate software);correct application of techniques and methods suitable for econometric research and the correct reporting thereof.Programming and interpreting computer output will be crucial and integral to the course. Stata and R will be used.
description.objectives: Upon completion of this course, the student: is able to analyse possible endogeneity;is able to use, evaluate, and judge appropriateness of econometric models for discrete choices and other limited dependent variables;is able to analyse linear and nonlinear models and methods;is able to use asymptotic and other theories to derive statistical properties for inference in linear and nonlinear models;is able to critically evaluate quantitative empirical economic research.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Econometrics and Data Science, B Actuarial Science, B Business Analytics, Pre-master Econometrics, Minor Actuarial Science (30 EC), Minor Econometrics and Mathematical Economics, or BSc Mathematics.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: This course builds on the subject Econometrics 1 (6 EC) and requires working knowledge gained in Econometrics 1. Knowledge and insights from mathematics and statistics are also constantly used so sufficient knowledge of the subjects in the courses Probability Theory and Statistics 3, Mathematics 3: Advanced Linear Algebra and Mathematics 4: Multivariate Analysis is necessary.

description.contents: During this course, applications in economics will be used to show how the knowledge acquired during the first two bachelor years can be applied in practice. We will focus on establishing causality in a regression and instrumental variable framework. Other contents of this course include:causality and the potential outcomes framework;threats to internal and external validity;implementation of research methods in Stata;the writing of a research paper;orally presenting research findings.
description.objectives: In the last 40 years, there have been massive innovations in computing technology as well as in the availability of data. This ignited the “credibility revolution” in economics in which the econometric toolbox is used to study the path from cause to effect. It teaches us how to approach questions like: “Does an econometrics degree lead to higher earnings?”, “Does competition in the healthcare market lead to better health?” or “Does working from home decrease productivity?”. This course applies econometric knowledge to real-world problems to obtain solid and sound empirical research findings about economic behaviour. At the end of this course, students will be able to:explain the difference between correlation and causality;analyse data and interpret research findings;critically assess threats to the internal and external validity of research designs;apply appropriate software (Stata);formulate the research findings in a written report as well as in an oral presentation;cooperate constructively within a team on a research project;make recommendations based on empirical research while considering the long-run implications of their recommendations;cooperate constructively within a diverse team.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Econometrics and Data Science, B Actuarial Science, BSc Mathematics, Pre-master Actuarial Science and Mathematical Finance, Pre-master Econometrics or Minor Econometrics and Mathematical Economics.

description.contents: This course covers basic mathematical and statistical models used in non-life insurance. Through utility theory, an economic motivation of insurance is given. Individual and collective risk models for the total claims in an insurance portfolio are discussed. Ruin theory, which gives insight into the long-term financial stability of an insurer, is covered. The Dutch bonus-malus system for automobile insurance is studied, including the Markov analysis needed for the determination of its asymptotic efficiency. The programming language R is used throughout to implement the models and techniques studied in the course.
description.objectives: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:explain the expected utility model as an economic model behind the insurance business;calculate or approximate the total claim size distribution in an insurance portfolio using individual and collective risk models;explain ruin theory as an economic model for an insurer's long-term financial stability;analyze the Markov chain structure of a bonus-malus system for automobile insurance;implement calculations and algorithms in risk theory using related built-in functions in R.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Econometrics and Data Science, B Actuarial Science, B Business Analytics, Pre-master Actuarial Science and Mathematical Finance, or the Minor Actuarial Science (30 EC).
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: This course has no subject-specific entry requirement. Having studied the courses Probability Theory and Statistics 2 and Probability Theory and Statistics 3 is recommended, not required.

description.contents: During the course, the theory of partial equilibrium is analysed using techniques and concepts from noncooperative game theory. The following issues will be discussed:partial equilibrium under perfect competition and monopoly;partial equilibrium under imperfect competition. Topics discussed are Nash-equilibrium, oligopoly, Cournot- and Bertrand competition, games in extensive form, subgame perfect Nash-equilibria, Stackelberg competition, horizontal differentiation;anticompetitive behaviour and competition policy. Topics discussed are entry deterrence, horizontal mergers, vertical integration, repeated games, tacit collusion, and the design of competition policy.
description.objectives: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:the student is able to explain the characteristics of the main forms of perfect and imperfect competition;the student is able to determine (subgame perfect) Nash equilibria in various models of oligopoly;the student is able to evaluate market outcomes on the basis of the efficiency of the resulting allocation;the student is able to explain theoretical arguments in the field of industrial organisation;the student can explain and calculate the impact of anti-competitive behavior;the student can explain the main competition policy designs.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Econometrics and Data Science, B Actuarial Science, B Business Analytics, BSc Mathematics, or the Minor Econometrics and Mathematical Economics.

description.contents: This course covers the univariate and multivariate time series analysis parts that are most relevant for analysing (macro)economic and financial time series.For univariate time series, these are:stationarity, ARMA models;unit root tests;Box-Jenkins method: identification, estimation and testing of ARIMA models;forecasting with ARIMA models;non-linear models, (G)ARCH models.For multivariate time series, the topics are:dynamic regressions, spurious regressions;vector autoregressive models, vector GARCH, and state space models;trend, cointegration and error correction models.Additional contemporaneous research topics will be covered, such as:nonlinear time series models;model averaging;density forecasts and their evaluation.The theory is applied in the context of practical examples using R.
description.objectives: Upon completion of this course, students will be able to:apply methods and techniques to identify, estimate and test models for univariate and multivariate time series;correctly interpret the results of methods applied to empirical time series;empirically evaluate the relative performance of competing forecasts;construct model confidence sets based on out-of-sample performance measures;use R to analyse time series.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Econometrics and Data Science, B Actuarial Science, B Business Analytics, B Mathematics.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: Mathematics 3: Advanced Linear Algebra or Mathematics 4: Multivariate Analysis + [Probability Theory and Statistics 3 or Econometrics 1]

description.contents: The methods taught will enable students to interpret relations among large amounts of microdata to help policymakers shape their strategies and economic policies. The contents of this course include:counterfactual framework, potential outcomes, average treatment effect (ATE);heterogeneous treatment effect with IVs, local average treatment effect (LATE);regression using panel data, fixed-effect model;difference-in-differences;regression discontinuity;synthetic control method;implementation of the above methods using R.
description.objectives: Modern microeconometrics based on individual, household, and establishment-level data greatly contribute to the greater availability of data from cross-section and longitudinal sample surveys and census data. This course provides a comprehensive treatment of the econometric analysis of such large micro datasets, intending to uncover patterns of economic behaviour. Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:apply panel data methods;understand the counterfactual framework, with potential outcomes;analyse large micro datasets;evaluate empirical cross-sectional and longitudinal studies;apply R programmes to cross-sectional and longitudinal samples.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Econometrics and Data Science and B Actuarial Science.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: This course builds on the subjects Econometrics 1 , Econometrics 2, and Empirical Project . Knowledge and insights from mathematics and statistics are also constantly used, so that sufficient knowledge of the subjects in the courses Probability Theory and Statistics 3, Mathematics 3: Advanced Linear Algebra, and Mathematics 4: Multivariate Analysis is necessary.

description.contents: The student works on an empirical or theoretical econometric or mathematical-economic project in this course. The subjects may concern different areas of economics such as labour economics (e.g. the effect of training), finance (for example, factor models for stock returns), macroeconomics (for example, cohesion prices and production) or mathematical economics (for example, price dynamics in a general equilibrium model, or game theory) or theoretical econometrics (e.g. simulation of a particular test) or big data. During the project, the student is guided in different ways. The research takes place under the regular supervision of a subject specialist. In addition, the student receives training in presentation skills and general and specific information about scientific research organisation. The research findings are recorded in an individual thesis of approximately twenty pages (excluding appendices). Furthermore, each student must hold two brief presentations, one in a group and one individually (about four minutes).
description.objectives: This is the skills part of the Bachelor Thesis Seminar, to be taken in parallel to Bachelor's Thesis Seminar Econometrics - Research Project. Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:formulate a clear and academic research question;critically evaluate academic literature;work in a professional and ethical matter;prepare and give a presentation on their own research;give feedback;write a report in academic style.
description.entryRequirements: Students must have obtained at least 120 credits (EC).

The research findings are recorded in an individual thesis of approximately twenty pages (excluding appendices). Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:formulate a clear and academic research question;critically evaluate academic literature;analyse economic data using quantitative methods;report (both written and orally) empirical or theoretical econometric or mathematical-economic scientific research;work in a professional and ethical matter;execute empirical or theoretical econometric or mathematical-economic scientific research;prepare and give a presentation on their own research.

progression: The first year has 60 EC and establishes calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, programming and quantitative economics. The first three teaching periods total 30 EC and the last three total 30 EC. The plan completes all first-year requirements.

The second year comprises 54 EC of common coursework and 6 EC of restricted choice. Risk Theory is first listed on the programme page and the dated catalogue confirms both options. Statistics 2 precedes Statistics 3 and machine learning. Econometrics 1 and 2 precede Empirical Project and underpin the later time-series and microeconometrics courses.

The third year first semester is 30 EC of approved choice; retain its scope without assuming particular modules or a placement. The second semester has 18 EC of Econometrics coursework and both 6 EC thesis seminar components. The completed first two years supply the 120 EC required by both thesis courses. The two credited components contribute to the same individual thesis, counted once as research.
